l: Theban resistance, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Alexander having quieted all the commotions in Greece, mardied
s: The Thebans resisted Alexander in defense of their liberty, recalling their earlier victories at Leuctra and Mantinea. Even after the city was taken, many continued fighting or refused to seek quarter.

l: Persian monarchy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Alexander having quieted all the commotions in Greece, mardied
s: Alexander's experienced army was intended, in his view, to end the Persian monarchy. He began planning the campaign after returning to Macedonia from the destruction of Thebes.

l: Asian expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Alexander having quieted all the commotions in Greece, mardied
s: After the campaign against Thebes, Alexander consulted his officers about an expedition into Asia, including when and how to begin it. He rejected advice to marry and secure an heir before undertaking the expedition, and then assembled his forces.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: Alexander crossed from Europe into Asia with a Macedonian army and claimed possession of Asia after landing at Troas. At the Granicus, the Macedonians defeated the Persian forces; Alexander killed Spithrobates and survived an attack by Rhosaces. Alexander then took Sardis and Miletus, dismissed most of his fleet, restored Ada to the rule of Caria, and besieged Halicarnassus. After fierce fighting, the Persian commanders abandoned Halicarnassus, and Alexander razed the city while the citadel remained defended.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: Alexander led his army across the Hellespont into Asia and claimed possession of the continent by casting his spear into the shore. He defeated the Persians at the Granicus, personally killed Spithrobates, and was slightly wounded by Rhosaces before Clitus saved him. He later took Sardis and Miletus, restored Ada to the rule of Caria, and captured and razed Halicarnassus.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: Asia was entered by Alexander’s army from Europe after the crossing of the Hellespont. Alexander symbolically claimed it as conquered by his spear and subsequently brought parts of its coast and inland regions under his power.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: The Macedonians crossed into Asia with Alexander and numbered about thirty thousand foot and four thousand five hundred horse according to the account. They defeated the Persian forces at the Granicus, took Miletus, and fought fiercely during the siege of Halicarnassus.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: The Persians assembled forces from many regions to oppose Alexander but rejected Memnon’s advice to avoid a direct battle. They were defeated at the Granicus, defended Miletus, and later resisted Alexander at Halicarnassus before abandoning the city.

l: Persian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: The Persian army at the Granicus included more than ten thousand horse and at least one hundred thousand foot. Its cavalry was routed by the Macedonians, after which the infantry fled; more than ten thousand foot were killed, at least two thousand horse were killed, and more than twenty thousand were taken prisoner.

l: Memnon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: Memnon the Rhodian advised the Persian commanders to destroy the country before Alexander and transfer the war to Macedonia, but they rejected his plan. He later commanded the defense of Halicarnassus, directed sallies against Alexander’s siege engines, and eventually left the city with the citizens and much of their wealth.

l: the river Granicus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: The Granicus was the river beside which the Persian forces encamped, using it as a defensive barrier. Alexander crossed it at daybreak, and the resulting battle ended in a Macedonian victory.

l: Battle of Granicus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: In the Battle of Granicus, Alexander crossed the river and attacked the Persian cavalry. The Persian horse and then the infantry were routed, while many Persian commanders were killed and large numbers of soldiers were killed or captured.

l: Spithrobates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: Spithrobates, the Persian governor of Ionia and son-in-law of Darius, led a force of horse against the Macedonians. He wounded Alexander with a javelin but was killed by Alexander, who pierced him through the head with a lance.

l: Miletus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: Miletus was defended by numerous soldiers and ample supplies, but Alexander breached its walls after attacking by land and sea. The Milesians surrendered themselves and the city; Alexander treated the Milesians mercifully but sold the other captured defenders into slavery.

l: Siege of Miletus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: During the Siege of Miletus, Alexander repeatedly assaulted the city and used engines to batter its walls. After the Macedonians forced a breach, the Milesians surrendered, and Alexander dismissed most of his fleet after the city was taken.

l: Halicarnassus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: Halicarnassus was the greatest city in Caria and contained a palace of the kings with turrets and citadels. After prolonged fighting, Memnon and the other commanders evacuated with many citizens and their wealth; Alexander then razed the city, while the citadel remained defended.

l: Siege of Halicarnassus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: During the Siege of Halicarnassus, Alexander attacked the walls, filled the trenches with machines called snails, and used rams to break down towers and walls. The defenders burned siege engines and resisted several assaults, but after Ephialtes was killed and the city was abandoned, Alexander surrounded the citadel and destroyed the city.

l: Caria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: Caria was entered by Alexander after he advanced along the coast of Asia. He gained cities there by surrender or storm, and he restored Ada, a woman of the Carian royal family, to the kingdom of her grandfather.

l: Ada, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: Ada, a noble woman of the Carian royal family, met Alexander while he was marching through Caria. After she asked him to restore her ancestral kingdom, Alexander gave it to her and thereby gained the support of the Grecian cities.

l: Battle of Granicus victory, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. It.
s: The Battle of Granicus victory was attributed above all to Alexander’s personal valor, with the Thessalian horse also receiving high praise. The victory opened the way for Alexander’s advance through Lydia to Sardis and onward against Miletus and Halicarnassus.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Chap. 11. DIODORUS SICULUS. 181
s: The unit is identified as Chapter 11, “Diodorus Siculus.” It is associated with page 181. No further readable information is provided.

l: Diodorus Siculus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, Chap. 11. DIODORUS SICULUS. 181
s: Diodorus Siculus is the subject identified in the chapter heading for Chapter 11. The heading places the chapter on page 181, but the unit provides no further readable information about him.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the utmost borders of Lycia, the Marmareofies*, who inha*
s: The Marmareofies, who inhabited a great fortified rock in the utmost borders of Lycia, attacked the rear of Alexander's army, killing many Macedonians and taking prisoners and carriage-horses. Alexander besieged the rock, but the Marmareofies resisted for two days and refused to make peace. Their leaders ultimately decided that the inhabitants should die and that the able young men should escape through the enemy's camp. The young men instead burned the houses and fled to the nearby mountains, making each house a sepulchre.

l: Marmareofies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the utmost borders of Lycia, the Marmareofies*, who inha*
s: The Marmareofies inhabited a great, well-fortified rock in Lycia. They attacked the rear of Alexander's army, killed many Macedonians, and carried away prisoners and carriage-horses before resisting Alexander's siege.

l: the fortified rock inhabited by the Marmareofies, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the utmost borders of Lycia, the Marmareofies*, who inha*
s: The rock was a great and well-fortified place that the Marmareofies defended against Alexander. It endured two days of continuous assault before the inhabitants resolved to abandon it through a desperate escape.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the utmost borders of Lycia, the Marmareofies*, who inha*
s: Alexander was enraged by the attack on his army and resolved to besiege the place. He used his utmost efforts to take the fortified rock and was said not to intend leaving until he had captured it.

l: Alexander's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the utmost borders of Lycia, the Marmareofies*, who inha*
s: Alexander's army was attacked in the rear by the Marmareofies while marching toward Lycia. Many Macedonians were killed, and prisoners and carriage-horses were taken.

l: the siege of the fortified rock, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the utmost borders of Lycia, the Marmareofies*, who inha*
s: The siege involved two days of uninterrupted assault. The Marmareofies resisted because they trusted in their valor and in the strength of the place.

l: the younger men, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the utmost borders of Lycia, the Marmareofies*, who inha*
s: The younger men initially rejected advice to make peace and resolved to surrender their lives and their country's liberty together. They approved the later counsel to burn the houses, and they broke through the enemy's camp and fled to the nearby hills.

l: the decree to kill the inhabitants and escape, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the utmost borders of Lycia, the Marmareofies*, who inha*
s: The older and graver men advised killing the old men, women, and children and having the able men break through the enemy's camp at night. An edict then directed everyone to return home, eat and drink with their families, and await the execution of the decree.

l: the burning of the houses, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the utmost borders of Lycia, the Marmareofies*, who inha*
s: Some of the younger men proposed burning the houses instead of killing their kindred with their own hands. This plan was agreed to and carried out, so that every man's house became his sepulchre.

l: the escape of the young men, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In the utmost borders of Lycia, the Marmareofies*, who inha*
s: The young men sallying from the gates broke through the midst of their enemies and fled to the hills near at hand. About six hundred young men were involved in this decision and escape.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Memnon, appointed by Darius to command the Persian forces, captured several cities and islands but died before invading Macedonia. Darius executed Charidemus the Athenian after rejecting his advice, then assembled a large army and marched toward Cilicia with his mother, wife, and children. Alexander recovered from a serious illness, seized Alexander of Lyncestes for investigation, and defeated Darius's army at Issus. Darius fled, while his mother, wife, son, and daughters were captured, and the Macedonians took the Persian camp and its treasures.

l: Memnon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Darius sent Memnon money and appointed him general of all his forces. Memnon raised troops, equipped three hundred ships, took several places in Chios and Lesbos, and gained alliances among the Cyclade islands, but he died of a mortal illness before completing his plans.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: After Memnon's death, Darius consulted his friends, rejected Charidemus's advice, and ordered Charidemus's execution. He gathered an army of four hundred thousand foot and one hundred thousand horse, marched toward Cilicia with his family, and was defeated at Issus, where he fled when his army broke.

l: Charidemus the Athenian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Charidemus advised Darius to remain in Asia and appoint an experienced general, arguing that one hundred thousand men would be sufficient. After calling Darius's advisers cowards, he was bound and delivered to the guards for execution.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Alexander was troubled by Memnon's successes but was relieved by Memnon's death. He recovered from a serious illness, sent Parmenio to secure the passes, seized Alexander of Lyncestes for trial, and defeated Darius at Issus after personally attacking him.

l: Philip of Acarnania, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Philip of Acarnania treated Alexander when other physicians considered him irrecoverable. His potion cured Alexander, and Alexander rewarded him generously and made him one of his most faithful friends.

l: Sisygambis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Darius's mother accompanied Darius's army toward Cilicia. She was captured after the battle at Issus and became part of the royal family whose condition moved the Macedonians to compassion.

l: Darius's wife, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Darius's wife accompanied the army with Darius. She was captured at Issus along with Darius's mother, children, and the rest of the royal household.

l: Darius's son, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Darius's son accompanied Darius's army. He was captured at Issus, and his misfortune especially drew tears from those who saw the royal family.

l: Darius's daughters, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Darius's two marriageable daughters accompanied the army. They were captured at Issus with their mother, grandmother, and brother.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: The Macedonians defeated the Persian army at Issus after fierce fighting. They pursued the Persians, took Darius's camp and treasures, and some treated the captive women brutally, while more moderate Macedonians pitied them.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: The Persians assembled a vast army under Darius and fought the Macedonians at Issus. After Darius was pressed by Alexander, the Persians began to flee, suffered heavy losses, and many escaped to allied cities.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Macedonia was threatened by Memnon's planned invasion and by reports that Greek forces might join the Persians. Alexander's recovery and victory at Issus prevented the immediate advance of that threat.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Darius hoped to transfer the war from Asia into Europe, but Memnon's death weakened that plan. After the battle at Issus, the text describes Asia as brought under the power of a conquering sword.

l: Cilicia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Darius marched toward Cilicia with his large army and family. Alexander seized Issus, a considerable city of Cilicia, before confronting Darius nearby.

l: Issus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Alexander possessed himself of Issus before the battle. The nearby battle at Issus ended in the defeat of Darius's army and the capture of Darius's family and camp.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: The Persian Empire was placed at great risk by the battle at Issus. Alexander believed that one victory could ruin the whole empire, and Darius's defeat greatly advanced that danger.

l: Persian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Darius's Persian army numbered four hundred thousand foot and one hundred thousand horse when it assembled at Babylon. It fought fiercely at Issus but collapsed after Darius came under intense pressure and fled.

l: Darius's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Darius's army marched from Babylon toward Cilicia after leaving its heavy baggage and rabble at Damascus. At Issus it fought the Macedonians, suffered extensive casualties, and lost its camp and royal household.

l: the battle at Issus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: The battle at Issus was fought between Alexander's Macedonians and Darius's Persians. Alexander attacked toward Darius, was wounded in the thigh, and helped force the Persian flight; the Persians lost more than one hundred and twenty thousand foot and ten thousand horse, while the Macedonians lost three hundred foot and one hundred and fifty horse.

l: Memnon's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Memnon's death stopped the progress of his successes and caused Darius's affairs to go backward. Darius had hoped that Memnon would carry the war from Asia into Europe, but afterward Darius was forced to prepare and lead the army himself.

l: Charidemus's execution, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Charidemus's execution followed his criticism of Darius's advisers and his advice that Darius should not personally risk the kingdom. Darius soon regretted the decision, but the execution could not be undone.

l: Alexander's illness, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Alexander fell desperately ill after hearing of Memnon's death. The physicians were afraid to treat him because they considered him irrecoverable.

l: Alexander's recovery, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Alexander recovered after Philip of Acarnania gave him a potion. He rewarded Philip generously and admitted him among his most faithful friends.

l: Alexander's seizure of Alexander of Lyncestes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: Alexander received letters from his mother warning him to be careful of Alexander of Lyncestes. After circumstances appeared to support an accusation, Alexander seized him and committed him to custody for legal trial.

l: the Persian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. III.
s: The Persian war continued after Memnon's death, with Darius assembling a vast army and Alexander advancing through Cilicia. The battle at Issus produced a major Macedonian victory, the capture of Darius's family, and the plundering of the Persian camp.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: After Darius and his army were routed, Darius fled toward the upper provinces, while Alexander pursued him for two hundred furlongs before returning to camp. When the women captives heard that Alexander had taken the spoils of Darius's tent, they mourned until Leonalus assured them that Darius was alive and that Alexander would respect their former dignity. The next morning Alexander visited the captives with Hephaestion and treated Sisygambis, Darius's wife, and Darius's little son with honor and kindness. Alexander restored the captives' royal privileges and promised to care for them, demonstrating the generosity and clemency for which the whole army praised him.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: After his army was routed, Darius fled rapidly, changing from one of his best horses to another in an effort to escape Alexander and reach the upper provinces. He remained alive, and Alexander assured the captives that he would respect their former dignity.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: Alexander pursued Darius closely with his best horsemen and chief friends, but returned to camp at midnight after riding two hundred furlongs. The next morning he visited the captives, treated them honorably, and promised to protect and provide for them.

l: Sisygambis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: Sisygambis, the mother of Darius, initially mistook Hephaestion for Alexander because Hephaestion was taller and more comely. After the mistake was revealed, Alexander lifted her up, called her mother, restored her royal robes and honors, and supplied her with attendants, servants, furniture, and additional provisions.

l: Hephaestion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: Hephaestion accompanied Alexander on his visit to the queens. Because he and Alexander were dressed alike and Hephaestion was taller and more comely, Sisygambis mistakenly took him for Alexander.

l: Darius's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: Darius's army was routed, causing Darius to flee. Its defeat enabled Alexander to take the rich spoils of Darius's tent.

l: the women captives, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: The women captives cried out and lamented when they heard that Darius had fled and that Alexander had taken the spoils of his tent. Their fears changed to joyful exultation after Leonalus assured them that Darius was alive and that Alexander would respect them, and they later praised Alexander's grace and clemency.

l: Darius's wife, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: Alexander declared that he would care for Darius's wife so that she would lack nothing needed to maintain her royal state and former prosperity.

l: Darius's little son, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: Alexander called Darius's little son to him and kissed him. He promised to educate him as carefully and honorably as if he were his own, and praised the six-year-old's brave and confident spirit.

l: the battle and rout, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: The battle resulted in the rout of Darius's army and the flight of Darius. Its outcome allowed Alexander to seize the rich spoils of Darius's tent.

l: Alexander's pursuit of Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: Alexander's pursuit carried him two hundred furlongs behind the fleeing Darius. He pursued Darius closely and earnestly desired to capture him, but returned to camp at midnight without becoming master of him.

l: Alexander's visit to the captives, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: Alexander visited the captives at first light with Hephaestion. He comforted Sisygambis after her mistaken obeisance, honored the women, kissed Darius's little son, and made promises concerning their protection, attendants, marriages, and support.

l: Alexander's generosity and clemency, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, But to return to the kings themselves : Darius with all his army
s: Alexander's generosity and clemency were shown by his respect for the captives' former dignity, restoration of Sisygambis's royal honors, provision of attendants and household goods, promises concerning the young ladies' marriages, and care for Darius's little son and wife. The army praised his incomparable grace and clemency, and the text presents this compassion toward the defeated as greater than victories achieved by fortune or valor alone.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As for Darius, being now got to Babylon, he mustered up his
s: Darius reached Babylon and mustered the broken troops that had escaped from the battle at Issus. He wrote to Alexander, offering ransom money for the captives and offering to give up part of Asia if Alexander would be his friend. Alexander showed selected letters to his council of war and dismissed the ambassadors without effect. Darius then prepared for war, raising an army that was twice the size of his force at Issus, with eight hundred thousand foot, two hundred thousand horse, and many hooked chariots.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As for Darius, being now got to Babylon, he mustered up his
s: Darius reached Babylon and mustered the broken troops that had escaped from the battle at Issus. Though he had suffered a great overthrow, he was not discouraged. He wrote to Alexander offering ransom money for the captives and part of Asia, then prepared extensively for war when the letters failed.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As for Darius, being now got to Babylon, he mustered up his
s: Babylon was the place Darius reached after the battle at Issus, where he mustered his broken troops.

l: broken troops, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As for Darius, being now got to Babylon, he mustered up his
s: The broken troops had escaped from the battle at Issus. Darius mustered them after reaching Babylon.

l: battle at Issus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As for Darius, being now got to Babylon, he mustered up his
s: The battle at Issus resulted in a great overthrow for Darius. Troops escaped from the battle and were later mustered by Darius at Babylon.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As for Darius, being now got to Babylon, he mustered up his
s: Alexander received letters from Darius and called a council of war. He showed the council the letters he judged most advantageous to himself while concealing the others, and the ambassadors were dismissed without effect.

l: letters from Darius to Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As for Darius, being now got to Babylon, he mustered up his
s: The letters advised Alexander to use his good fortune and success moderately. Darius offered a great sum of money for the ransom of the captives and offered to give Alexander part of Asia if he would be Darius's friend.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As for Darius, being now got to Babylon, he mustered up his
s: Darius offered to give Alexander all the part of Asia, with its cities, that lay on that side within the course of the river Halys, if Alexander would be his friend.

l: Alexander's Persian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As for Darius, being now got to Babylon, he mustered up his
s: After concluding that the matter could not be settled by letters, Darius prepared for war. He armed soldiers who had lost their weapons, raised others, formed them into regiments, and summoned forces left behind in the upper provinces.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: After the battle of Issus, Alexander marched toward Egypt and besieged Tyre, which refused him entry and resisted for seven months. The Macedonians built a mole to Tyre and eventually captured the city after overcoming extensive Tyrian defenses and naval resistance. The Tyrians suffered heavy losses, enslavement, and the execution of surviving young men, while Ballominus, a poor man of royal lineage, was made king of Tyre. Amyntas attempted to raise opposition to Alexander in Egypt but was defeated and killed, and the Greeks later sent ambassadors to congratulate Alexander on his victories, including the capture of Gaza.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Alexander marched toward Egypt after the battle of Issus and began the siege of Tyre when the city refused him entry to sacrifice to Hercules Tyrius. He directed the construction of the mole, led naval operations, personally mounted the Tyrian ramparts, and ultimately captured Tyre and Gaza.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The Tyrians resisted Alexander partly because they expected Darius to reward their loyalty and believed their resistance would give him time to recruit his army. Other survivors of the battle of Issus continued to support the Persian interest.

l: Hephaestion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Hephaestion was given authority to restore the kingdom of Tyre to one of Alexander's friends. He offered the principality to a wealthy citizen who declined it and then granted it to Ballominus, a poor man of royal lineage.

l: Ballominus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Ballominus was described as a prudent and good but extremely poor man of royal lineage. He was found drawing water for his hire, then was clothed in royal garments and publicly declared king of Tyre.

l: Amyntas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Amyntas, an exile from Macedonia, gathered mercenaries and sailed to Cyprus, Peloponnesus, and Egypt in support of Darius. He defeated the Egyptians near Memphis but was later killed with all his soldiers while they were scattered and plundering outside the city.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The Macedonians built and guarded the mole, attacked Tyre from land and sea, and repeatedly fought their way toward the walls despite severe losses. They eventually entered the city and captured it.

l: Tyrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The Tyrians refused Alexander entry, relying on their island's strength, abundant supplies, fleet, and connection with Carthage. They resisted the siege with numerous defensive inventions and fought until the city fell, after which thousands were killed, enslaved, or transported.

l: Phoenicians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The Phoenicians serving Tyre returned hurriedly to the city when Alexander attempted to enter its harbor. Some vessels were lost while forcing their way through the Macedonian fleet, and the Phoenicians continued to attack the besiegers with fire-darts, stones, and other weapons.

l: Issus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Issus is identified as the place of the battle preceding Alexander's march toward Egypt and the siege of Tyre. Survivors of the battle continued to organize resistance in support of Darius.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Alexander marched toward Egypt after the battle of Issus. Amyntas later entered Egypt with mercenaries, defeated the Egyptians near Memphis, and was then killed with his soldiers.

l: Phoenicia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: As Alexander entered Phoenicia on his way to Egypt, its other cities readily submitted to him and were received under his protection. Tyre was the exception.

l: Tyre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Tyre denied Alexander entry and endured a seven-month siege because it trusted its island position, supplies, fleet, and hoped-for Carthaginian support. Alexander eventually captured it, and the city suffered mass killing, enslavement, and the loss of its former ruler.

l: Gaza, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Gaza was a Persian garrison that Alexander besieged for two months and then took by assault. The Greek senate sent ambassadors to congratulate Alexander while he was at the siege.

l: battle at Issus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: After the battle of Issus, Alexander buried notable soldiers from both armies, rewarded his own troops, and allowed them time to rest. The battle also left Persian supporters and commanders attempting further resistance.

l: siege of Tyre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The siege of Tyre lasted seven months and involved attacks by land and sea, the construction of a mole, naval actions, storms, siege engines, and repeated close combat. Alexander ultimately refused to abandon the siege and captured the city.

l: fall of Tyre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: At the fall of Tyre, Macedonians entered through a breach and over the walls while the Tyrians continued fighting in the streets and narrow passages. More than seven thousand Tyrians were killed, the women and children were enslaved, and two thousand young men were hanged.

l: mole to Tyre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Alexander ordered the demolition of Old Tyre and used its stones to construct a mole two hundred feet wide toward the island city. Storms damaged it, but the Macedonians repaired and extended it until it reached the walls and supported their engines.

l: Tyrian fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: The Tyrians possessed a fleet of eighty ships and used it to attack the men working on the mole. Alexander later surrounded Tyre with his fleet and attempted to enter the harbor, while some Phoenician ships forced their way back into the city.

l: Tyrian defensive engines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Tyrian artificers devised wheels to shatter or deflect arrows and darts, wool packs to lessen the force of stones, hooks and nets to pull attackers from towers and bridges, and machines for throwing heated sand, iron, stones, and fire-darts. These devices killed or wounded many Macedonians and delayed the capture of the city.

l: Tyre's principality, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: After Tyre was captured, Alexander gave Hephaestion authority to assign its principality. Hephaestion first considered a wealthy citizen but ultimately awarded it to Ballominus, who was of royal lineage despite living in poverty.

l: Tyre's siege defenses, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IV.
s: Tyre's siege defenses included additional walls, plentiful supplies, a strong navy, skilled artificers, and many weapons and machines. The defenders reinforced damaged walls, blocked narrow passages, and fought fiercely from the walls, bridges, and streets.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: Alexander marched into Egypt, where the cities submitted to him, and then undertook a journey to the temple of Ammon. During the journey, rain, stored water, and crows helped Alexander and his companions cross the desert and reach the grove of Ammon. At the temple, the oracle declared Alexander divinely favored, promised him victory, and confirmed that Philip’s murderers had been punished. Alexander then returned to Egypt, founded Alexandria, and arranged its streets, walls, palace, and defenses.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: Alexander entered Egypt after the taking of Gaza, and the Egyptian cities submitted to him without fighting. He journeyed to the temple of Ammon, received favorable answers from its oracle, and then returned to Egypt to found Alexandria.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: Egypt submitted to Alexander after its cities rejected Persian rule. Alexander settled its affairs, returned there after visiting the temple of Ammon, and began building Alexandria.

l: temple of Ammon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: The temple of Ammon stood within a fertile, watered grove surrounded by a dry and sandy desert. Alexander visited it to consult the oracle and gave rich gifts after receiving favorable responses.

l: Jupiter Ammon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: Ammon was associated with a sacred grove, a temple, and an oracle visited by Alexander. The surrounding region included cities of Ammon and was inhabited by the Ammoni.

l: journey to the temple of Ammon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: During the journey to the temple of Ammon, Alexander was met by ambassadors from Cyrene and crossed a difficult desert. Rain relieved the travelers’ distress, and crows were said to guide them toward the temple.

l: desert, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: The desert surrounding the temple of Ammon was dry, scorching, sandy, and without a visible path. Alexander’s party crossed it by using water gathered from a valley, after rain had earlier supplied their immediate needs.

l: grove of Ammon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: The grove of Ammon was described as fifty furlongs broad and long, with pleasant fountains, running streams, and many fruit-bearing trees. Its air was said to have the character of constant spring despite the surrounding desert.

l: fountain of Solis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: The fountain of Solis stood outside the castle near the temple of Ammon. Its water changed temperature throughout the day, becoming coldest at noon and hottest around midnight before cooling again toward sunrise.

l: oracle of Ammon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: The oracle of Ammon told Alexander that he was the son of the god and would receive what he desired. It stated that Philip’s murderers had been punished and declared Alexander’s past successes evidence of divine birth and future victory.

l: Alexandria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CflAP. V.
s: Alexander founded Alexandria in Egypt between the marshes and the sea and named it after himself. He planned its streets, walls, defenses, palace, and harbor access, and the city was later enlarged by succeeding kings.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Darius assembled a vast army, equipped it with longer weapons and hooked chariots, and marched from Babylon toward Nineveh, encamping at Arbela. He made two peace offers to Alexander, but Alexander rejected them and demanded that Darius submit or fight for the empire. At the battle of Arbela, the Persian chariots initially terrified the Macedonians, but Alexander's countermeasure caused many to turn back or be destroyed. Alexander eventually routed Darius, although Mazaeus severely pressured the Macedonian wing before Parmenio rallied it; the Persians suffered over ninety thousand deaths, while the Macedonians lost about five hundred.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Darius gathered his forces, lengthened his swords and lances, prepared two hundred hooked chariots, and marched from Babylon with a very large army. He offered Alexander increasingly favorable peace terms, but after Alexander rejected them, he trained his soldiers and commanded the defense of the Tigris. During the battle, he fought from his chariot but fled after Alexander's attack caused his troops to believe he had been killed.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Alexander rejected Darius's peace proposals and demanded that Darius submit or fight for the whole empire. He crossed the Tigris with great difficulty, arranged his army to counter the hooked chariots, and commanded the right wing. He charged Darius, missed him with a dart but killed his chariot-driver, and later pursued the fleeing Persians.

l: Parmenio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Parmenio advised Alexander to accept Darius's peace terms if he were in Alexander's position. At the battle, he commanded Macedonian forces including the Thessalian horse, suffered severe pressure from Mazaeus, and eventually rallied his troops and helped defeat the Persians opposing him.

l: Mazaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Mazaeus was sent to guard the passage over the Tigris but abandoned that duty after judging the river impassable and instead destroyed the surrounding country. In the battle, he commanded Persian cavalry, supported the advance of the chariots, attacked the Macedonian wing, and sent Cadusian and Scythian horsemen around the enemy's wings to raid the Macedonian camp.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: The Persians fought with a very large and diverse army under Darius. Their chariots and cavalry initially put heavy pressure on the Macedonians, but Darius's flight caused their forces to disperse and they were ultimately defeated, suffering more than ninety thousand deaths.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: The Macedonians crossed the Tigris with great difficulty and prepared defensive measures against the hooked chariots. They were initially frightened and heavily pressed by Persian cavalry, but they disrupted most of the chariots, rallied after reverses, and defeated the Persians. About five hundred Macedonians were killed, though many were wounded.

l: Darius's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Darius's army consisted of about eight hundred thousand infantry and two hundred thousand cavalry drawn from many nations. It trained at Arbela, advanced against Alexander, initially gained advantages on parts of the field, and then collapsed after Darius fled.

l: Alexander's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Alexander's army crossed the Tigris and encamped near the Persian force before forming for battle with cavalry in front. Its wings were arranged in a half-moon, and its infantry used noise and open formations to counter the hooked chariots. It ultimately defeated the Persian army despite suffering serious pressure on one wing.

l: Nineveh, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Nineveh was the large, open country that Darius intended to reach for the battle because it was considered suitable for deploying his enormous army.

l: Arbela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Arbela was a village where Darius encamped and trained his army. The battle later fought near this place was called the battle of Arbela.

l: Tigris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: The Tigris lay to Darius's right during his march. Darius intended to use it as a defense, but Alexander found a ford and crossed it with great toil and danger.

l: battle at Arbela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: The battle of Arbela was fought between Alexander's Macedonians and Darius's Persians after both sides assembled their forces near Arbela. Alexander's forces eventually prevailed after Darius fled, although Mazaeus's cavalry inflicted severe losses and forced part of the Macedonian army to retreat.

l: peace negotiations between Darius and Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Darius conducted two attempts to negotiate peace with Alexander. He first offered the lands within the Halys and two thousand talents of silver, then offered the lands within the Euphrates, three thousand talents, one of his daughters in marriage, and a partnership in the kingdom; Alexander rejected both proposals.

l: hooked chariots, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: Darius prepared two hundred hooked chariots fitted with darts, longer blades, and sharp hooks intended to terrify and cut down enemy soldiers. Alexander ordered his infantry to strike their shields with javelins to frighten the horses and to open their ranks if the chariots continued forward.

l: Persian chariot force, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: The Persian chariot force advanced with great power and initially amazed and terrified the Macedonians. The noise made by the Macedonian infantry caused many chariots to turn back into the Persian army, while others were destroyed, diverted, or forced through the infantry with deadly effect.

l: Persian army's peace offer, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, As soon as Darius had intelligence of his coming, he got all his
s: The Persian army's peace offer promised Alexander territory, silver, marriage to one of Darius's daughters, and a share in the kingdom if he accepted Darius's terms. Alexander refused, declaring that two kings could not reign together and ordering the ambassadors to tell Darius either to fight for the empire or submit.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: After Alexander's victory at Arbela, many Grecians conspired to revolt and resolved to aid Darius with money for foreign soldiers. Memnon rebelled in Thrace, prompting Antipater to settle matters there and march into Greece. The Lacedaemonians formed a confederate league with many Peloponnesians and others, raised an army under Agis, and fought Antipater. Agis was killed, and the Lacedaemonians and their allies were defeated and retreated toward Sparta.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: His victory at Arbela encouraged many cities of Greece to prepare to defend their ancient liberties. The Grecians believed that he would not divide his army lest he disturb them.

l: Memnon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Sent as general into Thrace, Memnon rebelled at the instigation of the barbarians and appeared in open war with a great army.

l: Antipater, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Antipater gathered his forces and marched through Macedonia into Thrace against Memnon. After hearing of the Grecian defection, he settled matters relating to the war in Thrace as well as he could and marched with his forces into Greece, where he defeated the confederates.

l: Agis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Agis was made general of the Lacedaemonians and their confederates. He fought with great valor and resolution, received many wounds, ordered his soldiers to leave him and preserve themselves for future service, and died fighting after being shot through the body with a dart.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Many Grecians resolved to assist Darius with money to raise foreign soldiers. Many Peloponnesians and others joined the league, but the Athenians remained quiet and firm in their duty to Alexander.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Lacedaemonians judged that the insurrection in Thrace offered an opportunity for war and solicited the Grecians to confederate for their remaining liberties. They led the war under Agis, were defeated by Antipater, and retreated toward Sparta.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Many cities of Greece began preparing to defend their ancient liberties after hearing of the victory at Arbela. Antipater later marched with his forces into Greece.

l: Thrace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Thrace was the scene of Memnon's rebellion and of Antipater's initial campaign against him. Antipater settled matters there as well as he could before marching into Greece.

l: Memnon's rebellion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Memnon's rebellion created an open war in Thrace and encouraged the Grecians to revolt. Antipater responded by gathering his forces and marching against Memnon.

l: insurrection in Thrace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The insurrection in Thrace encouraged the Lacedaemonians and other Grecians to prepare for war and revolt.

l: Grecian revolt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The Grecian revolt followed the victory at Arbela and the insurrection in Thrace. The Grecians sought to aid Darius, while Antipater marched into Greece against them.

l: confederate league, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Many Peloponnesians and some others entered the confederate league and enrolled as soldiers. They raised an army of twenty thousand infantry and two thousand cavalry, placing its management with the Lacedaemonians.

l: war in Thrace, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: The war in Thrace began after Memnon rebelled there. Antipater composed its affairs as well as he could before marching into Greece.

l: ancient liberties of Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VI.
s: Many cities of Greece sought to defend their ancient liberties while the Persians still had power to assist them. The Lacedaemonians called upon the Grecians to unite for their remaining liberties.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: After defeating Darius at Arbela, Alexander entered Babylon, distributed money to his troops, and marched through Sitacana, Susa, and the country of the Usians toward Persepolis. He overcame the defenders of the Susian Rocks, received the surrender of Persepolis, rewarded nearly eight hundred maimed Greek captives, and gave the city to his soldiers for plunder. Alexander seized the immense Persian treasury and the treasures of the Persepolis citadel, then held a feast at which Thais persuaded him to burn the palace. Darius fled toward Bactria and was treacherously murdered by Bessus before Alexander found his body and had it honorably buried.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: After the Battle of Arbela, Alexander entered Babylon, refreshed his army, appointed governors, and distributed money to his troops. He then marched through Sitacana, Susa, the country of the Usians, and the Susian Rocks toward Persepolis, rewarding a guide who enabled him to defeat the defenders. At Persepolis he aided the maimed Greek captives, gave the city to the Macedonians for plunder, seized the Persian treasury, held a feast, and led the burning of the palace.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: After being routed at Arbela, Darius fled toward the higher provinces and attempted to raise another army. He later withdrew from Bactria with Persians and mercenary Greeks, but was treacherously murdered by Bessus. Alexander found his body and had it honorably interred.

l: Arbela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: Arbela was the place where Darius was routed. Alexander entered it after burying those killed in the battle and found rich royal furniture and treasures amounting to three thousand talents of silver.

l: battle at Arbela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: The Battle of Arbela ended in Darius's defeat and flight. Afterward, Alexander buried the dead before entering Arbela.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: Babylon received Alexander cheerfully and provided splendid entertainment for the Macedonians. Alexander remained there for more than thirty days, appointed governors and a castle commander, distributed money to his troops, and ordered forces and transport to be supplied from the city.

l: Sitacana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: Alexander reached Sitacana after six marches and stayed there for several days. He used the province to refresh his soldiers, review his army, promote deserving officers, and improve military discipline.

l: Susa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: Susa, the royal city of Susiana, was voluntarily surrendered to Alexander by Abulites. Alexander found more than forty thousand talents of uncoined gold and silver and nine thousand talents in coined money there, left Darius's family at Susa, and later ordered part of the Persian treasury to be stored there.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: Persia was invaded by Alexander after the defeat of Darius. Its cities and royal treasures were taken, Persepolis was plundered and burned, and Darius was later murdered while fleeing through the Persian territories.

l: Persepolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: Persepolis was the metropolis of the Persian kingdom and was described as the richest city in Asia. Alexander gave it to the Macedonians to plunder, after which its men were killed, its property was seized, and its palace was burned.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: The Greeks were described as having suffered greatly under the Persian kings, including the destruction of their temples. Alexander encountered nearly eight hundred Greek captives who had been enslaved and mutilated by the Persians.

l: maimed Greek captives, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: The maimed Greek captives, mostly old men, had suffered the loss of hands, feet, ears, noses, or other bodily parts under the Persian kings. They asked Alexander for aid and chose to remain together rather than return to Greece; Alexander gave each man three thousand drachmas, clothing, oxen, sheep, grain, and freedom from taxes and tribute.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: The Macedonians were entertained at Babylon and received payments from Alexander. At Persepolis they plundered the city, killed its men, fought among themselves over the spoils, enslaved women, and joined Alexander in burning the palace.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: The Persians defended the passes and opposed Alexander in the country leading toward Persepolis. They had mutilated and enslaved Greek captives, and thirty thousand Persians and mercenary Greeks accompanied Darius when he fled from Bactria.

l: Persian treasury, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: The Persian treasury included vast accumulated wealth. Alexander found more than forty thousand talents of uncoined gold and silver at Susa, nine thousand talents in coined money, and ordered the treasure taken from Persepolis to be divided between military use and storage at Susa.

l: Persepolis citadel, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: The Persepolis citadel contained a vast public treasury collected from the time of Cyrus, amounting to one hundred and twenty thousand talents when the gold was reckoned as silver. It was surrounded by three walls, included royal and military buildings and treasury chambers, and was consumed by fire after the feast.

l: Alexander's feast at Persepolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: Alexander held a sumptuous feast at Persepolis for his friends, celebrated his victory, and offered sacrifices to the gods. The feast became disorderly through drinking and debauchery, and the proposal to burn the palace was made and accepted there.

l: Thais, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: Thais was an Athenian courtesan present at Alexander's feast at Persepolis. She urged Alexander to burn the palace so that Persia's glory would be destroyed by the hands of women, and she threw the first firebrand into it.

l: burning of Persepolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: The burning of Persepolis was carried out after Thais proposed it during Alexander's feast. Alexander led the procession, Thais threw the first firebrand, and the palace was soon consumed to ashes; the act was presented as revenge for Xerxes's destruction of the citadel of Athens.

l: Bessus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: Bessus was the lord-lieutenant of Bactria. He treacherously murdered Darius while Darius was fleeing from Alexander.

l: Darius's murder, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VU.
s: Darius's murder was committed treacherously by Bessus during Darius's retreat from Bactria. Alexander soon reached the place where Darius lay and had him honorably buried; another account says Darius was still alive long enough to ask Alexander to avenge him.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In Europe, the Lacedtemoniaus being routed in a great battle by
s: The Lacedemonians were routed by Antipater in a great battle and were forced to send ambassadors to him. Antipater postponed their appeal until the general assembly of Greece met at Corinth. After disputes on both sides, the matter was left to Alexander's decision. Antipater received the chiefest of the nobility of Sparta as hostages, and the Lacedemonians sent ambassadors into Asia to beg pardon for their late revolt.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In Europe, the Lacedtemoniaus being routed in a great battle by
s: The Lacedemonians were routed by Antipater in a great battle and were forced to send ambassadors to him. They later sent ambassadors into Asia to beg pardon for their late revolt.

l: Antipater, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In Europe, the Lacedtemoniaus being routed in a great battle by
s: Antipater routed the Lacedemonians in a great battle. He postponed their ambassadors' appeal until the general assembly of Greece met at Corinth and received the chiefest of the nobility of Sparta as hostages.

l: great battle, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In Europe, the Lacedtemoniaus being routed in a great battle by
s: The great battle was the battle in which Antipater routed the Lacedemonians.

l: ambassadors (the Lacedemonians' ambassadors), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In Europe, the Lacedtemoniaus being routed in a great battle by
s: The Lacedemonians' ambassadors were sent to Antipater after the Lacedemonians were routed. They were put off until the general assembly of Greece met at Corinth, and other ambassadors were later sent into Asia to beg pardon for the late revolt.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In Europe, the Lacedtemoniaus being routed in a great battle by
s: The matter disputed at Corinth was left to Alexander's decision.

l: chiefest of the nobility of Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In Europe, the Lacedtemoniaus being routed in a great battle by
s: The chiefest of the nobility of Sparta were received by Antipater as hostages.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In Europe, the Lacedtemoniaus being routed in a great battle by
s: Sparta was associated with the chiefest of its nobility, whom Antipater received as hostages.

l: hostages (the chiefest of the nobility of Sparta), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In Europe, the Lacedtemoniaus being routed in a great battle by
s: The chiefest of the nobility of Sparta served as hostages received by Antipater.

l: late revolt of the Lacedemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, In Europe, the Lacedtemoniaus being routed in a great battle by
s: The late revolt of the Lacedemonians was the reason for which they sent ambassadors into Asia to beg pardon.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Bessus, Nabarzanes, and Barzaentes flee to Bactria after Darius's death, and Bessus raises an uprising by persuading the Bactrians to claim their liberty and recognize him as king. Alexander rewards and dismisses the Greek auxiliaries, campaigns through Hyrcania and the Mardian country, recovers his war horse, and receives Thalestris, queen of the Amazons. Alexander adopts elements of Persian royal dress and courtly customs before dealing with rebellions and a plot involving Dimnus, Ceballinus, Philotas, and others. He then campaigns against the Arimaspi, appoints Teridates over the Arimaspi and Gedrosians, and subdues Arachosia.

l: Bessus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Bessus escaped after the death of Darius and went to Bactria with Nabarzanes, Barzaentes, and others. Because he had been appointed lord-lieutenant of Bactria by Darius and was well known there, he persuaded the inhabitants to resist Alexander, organized forces and supplies, and was recognized by many as king.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Darius had appointed Bessus lord-lieutenant of Bactria. After Darius's death, Bessus and other supporters escaped Alexander and continued resistance against him.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: The Macedonians wanted to end the war with the death of Darius and return home. Alexander persuaded them to continue the remaining expeditions, and later separated those who complained about Parmenio's death or criticized him into a unit called the Unruly Company.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Alexander persuaded the Macedonians to continue the war, rewarded and discharged the Greek auxiliaries, and conquered or secured territories in Hyrcania, the Mardian country, Drangina, and Arachosia. He recovered his war horse, received Thalestris, adopted some Persian customs and court practices, punished alleged conspirators, and campaigned against the Arimaspi.

l: Greek auxiliaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Alexander praised the Greek auxiliaries for their valor, paid each horseman a talent and each foot soldier ten minas, settled their arrears and travel provisions, and discharged them from further service. Those who chose to remain in the army received three talents each.

l: Hyrcania, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Alexander entered Hyrcania, gained its towns and cities as far as the Caspian Sea, and traveled through its sea-coasts and bordering country. The text describes Hyrcania as exceptionally fertile and rich, with abundant vines, fig trees, honey-producing trees, and the Anthredon insect.

l: horse (Alexander's war horse), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Alexander's best horse had been given to him by Demaratus the Corinthian and had carried him in all his battles in Asia. It recognized Alexander, knelt for him to mount, and was captured by the barbarians in the Mardian country before being restored.

l: Thalestris, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Thalestris, queen of the Amazons, met Alexander in Hyrcania with three hundred Amazons. She said that she had come to have a child by him, and after spending thirteen days with him she received honorable gifts and returned to her kingdom.

l: Amazons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: The Amazons were represented by Thalestris, their queen, who came to Alexander with three hundred women in warlike dress. Their dominions were said to lie between the Phasis and the Thermodon.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Alexander began imitating the luxury and effeminate manners attributed to the Persians. He adopted Persian dress and court practices, though the text says he used some of these customs sparingly so as not to offend the Macedonians.

l: Persianization of Alexander's court, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Alexander ordered the officers of his court to be Asiatics and made Asian nobles squires of the body, including Oxathres, the brother of Darius. He wore the Persian diadem and other Persian clothing, gave purple gowns to his friends, dressed his horsemen in Persian habit, and brought concubines with him.

l: Satibarzanes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Satibarzanes killed the soldiers placed under his command and joined Bessus in plotting war against the Macedonians. When Alexander approached Chrotacana, Satibarzanes fled with two thousand horse to seek help from Bessus, while his remaining forces were forced to surrender; later, he was reported to have entered the country of the Arians with a large body of cavalry and withdrawn its inhabitants from Alexander's allegiance.

l: Drangiana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Alexander entered Drangina and encamped at its royal city to refresh his army. A plot against him was uncovered there, and after settling his affairs in the province he marched against the Arimaspi.

l: Dimnus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Dimnus, one of Alexander's friends, became enraged with the king and planned to assassinate him. After the plot was exposed, Dimnus stabbed himself.

l: Ceballinus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Ceballinus learned of the assassination plot from his brother Nicomachus. When Philotas delayed reporting it, Ceballinus told one of the king's pages, hid in the armory, and thereby helped bring the conspiracy to Alexander's attention.

l: Philotas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Philotas was informed by Ceballinus about the plot but failed to report it promptly to Alexander. He denied participation but was condemned by the Macedonians, later confessed the whole plot under torture, and was executed with the other conspirators.

l: Parmenio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Parmenio was regarded as one of Alexander's most faithful friends, but he was suspected of managing the conspiracy through his son Philotas. Alexander had him seized unexpectedly at Ecbatana, where he governed Media and guarded the royal treasures, and Parmenio was put to death.

l: Arimaspi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: The Arimaspi, later called Evergetae, were said to have once brought Cyrus thirty thousand carts and wagons loaded with provisions when his army was in extreme need. Alexander marched against them, but they received him favorably, and he granted them marks of his grace and favor.

l: Bessus's Bactrian uprising, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Bessus used his former position as Darius's lord-lieutenant and his familiarity with the inhabitants to raise resistance in Bactria. He persuaded many Bactrians to claim liberty, recognized him as king, and helped organize men, weapons, and supplies.

l: recovery of Alexander's horse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: After Alexander's war horse was captured by the Mardians, Alexander threatened to destroy their country with fire and sword and began carrying out the threat. The terrified barbarians restored the horse, brought rich gifts, sent fifty ambassadors, and begged Alexander's pardon; he accepted some of their leading men as hostages.

l: plot against Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: Dimnus planned to assassinate Alexander and tried to recruit Nicomachus. Nicomachus told Ceballinus, who eventually informed a king's page; the plot was investigated, Dimnus killed himself, and Philotas and other alleged conspirators were condemned and executed.

l: Philotas's execution, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: The Macedonians examined the conspiracy and condemned Philotas and the other conspirators to death. Philotas confessed under torture, and he and the others were executed according to the custom of their country; Alexander Lyncestes was executed at the same time.

l: Alexander's campaign against the Arimaspi, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: After settling affairs in Drangina, Alexander marched against the Arimaspi, who were also called Evergetae. They received him with love and kindness, and Alexander rewarded them; he also showed favor to the neighboring Gedrosians and appointed Teridates governor over both peoples.

l: subjugation of Arachosia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. VIII.
s: While Satibarzanes was reported to be stirring up the Arians, Alexander himself subdued Arachosia and caused its people to submit to his government.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Alexander led the Macedonians through the snowy country of the Paropamisadae, crossed Caucasus, founded Alexandria and other cities, and then marched toward Bactria. Satibarzanes was killed in single combat by Erigyus, while Bessus was captured by his own commanders and delivered to Alexander for punishment. In India, Alexander massacred the Massaga mercenaries after they had surrendered their city and captured the supposedly impregnable rock of Aornos. After crossing the Indus, Alexander received Mophis, also called Taxiles, as a submissive ally and restored him to his kingdom.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Alexander led his army against the Paropamisadae, endured severe snow and cold, crossed Caucasus in sixteen days, and founded Alexandria and other cities. He then marched toward Bactria, where Bessus had usurped the crown, and later campaigned in India, massacring the Massaga mercenaries, capturing Aornos, crossing the Indus, and receiving Mophis into his protection.

l: Paropamisadae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: The Paropamisadae lay far to the north and were covered with snow, with severe cold that made travel difficult. Their inhabitants lived in tightly built, spired-roofed houses, stored provisions for the long winter, and surrendered after Alexander captured their towns.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: The Macedonians followed Alexander through the snowy Paropamisadae, although some stragglers were left behind and others were blinded or killed by the reflected brightness of the snow. They fought the Massaga mercenaries and took part in the assault on Aornos.

l: Caucasus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Caucasus, also called Paropamisus by some, was crossed by Alexander in a sixteen-day march. Near its foot he founded Alexandria, and the text identifies a rock there with the supposed cave and fetters of Prometheus.

l: Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Alexander marched into Bactria after hearing that Bessus had usurped the crown and raised a numerous army.

l: Bessus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Bessus took the name of king and quarreled with Bagodares while drinking. After Bagodares fled to Alexander, Bessus's commanders conspired against him, seized him, and delivered him to Alexander, who handed him over to Darius's brother and kindred; they tortured and killed him.

l: Satibarzanes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Satibarzanes commanded a strong army in Aria and fought Alexander's commanders. During a general battle he removed his helmet and challenged an enemy commander to single combat, but Erigyus killed him, causing his forces to surrender.

l: Massaga mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: The Massaga mercenaries left their city under an agreement and marched eight hundred furlongs without suspecting danger. Alexander then attacked them unexpectedly; they formed a defensive ring around their families and fought until the men and many women were killed, after which the unarmed survivors and remaining women were given to his horsemen.

l: Aornos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Aornos was a strongly fortified rock where surviving inhabitants took refuge; it was about one hundred furlongs around and sixteen furlongs high, with the Indus running below its southern side. Guided by an old man, Alexander blocked its only passage, raised a mount, and forced the defenders to abandon it during the night.

l: Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: The Indus ran at the southern foot of Aornos and was described as the greatest river of India. After reaching it, Alexander used ships with thirty oars apiece to make a bridge, rested his army there for thirty days, and offered sacrifices to the gods.

l: Indians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: The Indians defending Aornos were frightened by the Macedonian assault and abandoned the rock during the night. Elsewhere, Indians killed Aphrices, brought his head to Alexander, and were received into his protection.

l: Taxiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Taxiles had formerly reigned in the country beyond the Indus, and after his death his son Mophis succeeded him. At the end of the account, Mophis is also called Taxiles and is described as becoming Alexander's constant and faithful friend and associate.

l: Mophis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Mophis sent an ambassador to Alexander in Sogdiana, offering assistance against the Indians and promising to surrender his kingdom. When he approached Alexander with an army and elephants, Alexander initially mistook the movement for treachery, but Mophis halted his army and delivered himself and his forces to the king; Alexander restored him to his kingdom.

l: Alexandrian campaign in India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: In the Indian campaign, Alexander pursued the Massaga mercenaries, took several opposing cities, captured Aornos, crossed the Indus, and received Indian forces and elephants into his protection. The campaign also brought him into alliance with Mophis, whom he restored to his kingdom.

l: massacre of the Massaga mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: After the Massaga mercenaries had been allowed to leave their city, Alexander pursued and attacked them without warning. The mercenaries and their wives resisted in a circular formation but were overwhelmed, and the unarmed survivors and remaining women were distributed among Alexander's horsemen.

l: siege and capture of Aornos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Alexander learned the approaches to Aornos from an old man who lived nearby, seized the only passage to the summit, and built a mount toward the fort. After seven days of continuous assault, he withdrew the guard blocking the passage, and the defenders fled by night, leaving Alexander in possession of the rock.

l: Mophis's submission to Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. IX.
s: Mophis approached Alexander with a well-equipped army and elephants after previously promising assistance and the surrender of his kingdom. Although Alexander first suspected an attack, Mophis halted his forces and surrendered himself and his army; Alexander rewarded the submission by restoring him to his kingdom.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: Alexander refreshed his army in the province of Taxiles and marched against Porus, prince of the neighboring Indians, whose army included more than fifty thousand foot soldiers, three thousand horse, over a thousand chariots, and 130 elephants. In the battle between Alexander and Porus, the Macedonians overcame the Indian chariots and elephants, and Porus was wounded and captured after fighting bravely. Alexander won the victory, restored Porus to his kingdom after he recovered, compelled Embisarus to submit, and allowed his army to rest for thirty days. Alexander crossed the river Hydaspes, built two cities near the crossing and battlefield, and learned of the region's enormous trees, giant serpents, apes, and poisonous snakes.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: Alexander refreshed his army in Taxiles and marched against Porus. He defeated the Indian army, compelled Embisarus to submit, built two cities near the river, restored Porus to his kingdom after his recovery, and allowed his army to rest for thirty days.

l: Porus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: Porus commanded an army containing infantry, horse, chariots, and elephants against Alexander. He fought with great strength and courage, was wounded by many darts and arrows, fell from his elephant, and was captured while still alive. After recovering, he was restored by Alexander to his kingdom.

l: Embisarus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: Embisarus was a neighboring king whose power was said to be no less than Porus's. Because he had been slow to assist Porus and was frightened after the battle, Alexander compelled him to submit.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Macedonians endured the attacks of the Indian elephants and killed the soldiers guarding them with their sarissas. They suffered the loss of 280 horsemen and more than 700 foot soldiers, while Alexander arranged for the dead to be decently buried and rewarded survivors who had shown valor.

l: Indians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Indians fought Alexander under Porus and lost more than twelve thousand men, including two sons of Porus, army generals, and leading commanders. More than nine thousand Indians were taken prisoner.

l: Taxiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
