s: Taxiles was the province where Alexander refreshed his army before marching against Porus.

l: India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: India is described as the region in which Porus and Embisarus ruled neighboring kingdoms. Alexander intended to continue through India to its utmost bounds and then pass by the river into the ocean.

l: Hydaspes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The river Hydaspes was near the battlefield and was crossed by Alexander's forces. Alexander built one city on the farther side of the river where his army passed over and another where he overcame Porus.

l: battle of Alexander and Porus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: In the battle, Alexander's horse first broke the Indian chariots, while the elephants caused severe losses among the Macedonians. The Macedonians then killed the elephant guards and wounded the elephants until they panicked and trampled Indian soldiers. Porus made a fierce charge with forty elephants before he was overcome.

l: Alexander's victory over Porus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: Alexander's victory caused the remaining Indians to flee and resulted in a great slaughter. Alexander took prisoners and elephants, sacrificed to the sun for the victory, and restored the wounded Porus to his kingdom after he recovered.

l: Alexander's crossing of the Hydaspes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: Alexander crossed the river Hydaspes with his forces. He built a city on the farther side of the river at the crossing and another at the place where he defeated Porus.

l: elephants, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: Porus's army used more than a hundred elephants, placing them at equal distances in front and protecting them with armed men. The elephants crushed, trampled, seized, and threw Macedonians, but after being struck by many darts they panicked, broke formation, and trampled their own soldiers.

l: Indian army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, CHAP. X.
s: The Indian army under Porus had more than fifty thousand foot soldiers, three thousand horse, over a thousand chariots, and 130 elephants. It lost more than twelve thousand men, including important commanders, and more than nine thousand soldiers were captured.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Alexander continued his campaign in India, sending Hephastion to subdue a neighboring prince’s kingdom for Porus while conquering territories including those of the Audrastians and Cathari. He received the submission of Sopithes and Phigeus, learned from Phigeus and Porus about the Ganges and the powerful Gandarites, and considered invading them despite the exhaustion of his army. During the advance he witnessed Dioxippus defeat the Macedonian Coragus, though Dioxippus later killed himself after being falsely accused of theft. Alexander’s river voyage was endangered by whirlpools, and during the siege of the Oxydracee and Mallii capital he was severely wounded before being rescued by his guards.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Alexander continued conquering Indian territories, accepted the submission of Sopithes and Phigeus, and considered an invasion of the Gandarites despite his army’s exhaustion. He survived dangerous river whirlpools and personally led the assault on the capital city of the Oxydracee and Mallii, where he was severely wounded but rescued.

l: Porus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Porus received the kingdom of the neighboring prince after Hephastion subdued it for Alexander. Alexander later questioned Porus about the reported strength of the Gandarites, and Porus confirmed the report.

l: Gandarites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: The Gandarites were reported to live beyond the Ganges and to be ruled by Xandrames. Their king was said to command twenty thousand horse, two hundred thousand foot, two thousand chariots, and four thousand elephants.

l: Sopithes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Sopithes ruled cities governed by laws that emphasized physical beauty, health, and strength. He surrendered himself and his kingdom to Alexander, received the kingdom back, entertained Alexander’s army, and presented Alexander with one hundred and fifty exceptionally large and strong dogs.

l: Hydaspes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: The Hydaspes was described as seven furlongs wide, six fathoms deep, and a fierce, difficult river to cross. Alexander later moved toward it after being entertained by Phigeus.

l: Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: The Indus was one of the great rivers whose waters met other rivers and formed dangerous whirlpools. Alexander’s fleet later sailed down the river system, and his ship was caught in one of the whirlpools.

l: Ganges, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: The Ganges was reported to lie beyond a twelve-day desert and to be twenty-two furlongs wide and the deepest river in India. The Gandarites were said to dwell beyond it.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: The Macedonians continued campaigning despite severe exhaustion, worn-out equipment, damaged horse hooves, and clothing made from Indian material. They later suffered losses in the river voyage and, after Alexander was wounded, massacred the men found in the captured city.

l: Indians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Indians resisted Alexander in several towns and fought from rooftops during the capture of a city. During the siege of the Oxydracee and Mallii capital, they surrounded and wounded Alexander before his troops rescued him.

l: Dioxippus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Dioxippus defeated the Macedonian Coragus in single combat by breaking his sarissa and knocking him down with a blow. After being falsely accused of stealing a golden cup, he wrote to Alexander and then killed himself.

l: Oxydracee, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: The Oxydracee were a populous and warlike Indian nation that joined with the Mallii against Alexander. Their capital city was besieged and captured after Alexander was wounded during the assault.

l: Mallii, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: The Mallii were a populous and warlike Indian nation that confederated with the Oxydracee against Alexander. Their capital city was assaulted and taken, after which the Macedonians killed the men they found there.

l: capital city of the Oxydracee and Mallii, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: The capital city was targeted by Alexander without delay despite a soothsayer’s warning that he would be wounded. Alexander entered through the gate, climbed the wall, was left isolated when the ladders broke, and was struck by a severe wound before being rescued.

l: Alexander's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Alexander’s army had campaigned for eight years and was worn down by continuous marches, losses, damaged weapons, exhausted horses, and prolonged storms. Alexander attempted to secure its support for the invasion of the Gandarites through speeches, plunder, and gifts of food to the soldiers’ families.

l: soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: The soldiers were described as exhausted and poorly equipped after years of campaigning. Their wives and children were gathered by Alexander, and corn was ordered to be distributed monthly among the wives.

l: conquest of India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: The conquest continued through the submission or capture of numerous Indian territories and cities. Hephastion was praised after subduing a great part of India, while Alexander continued toward the Oxydracee and Mallii.

l: invasion of the Gandarites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Alexander wished to invade the Gandarites after hearing of their powerful army beyond the Ganges. He recognized the expedition’s difficulty but initially intended to proceed, although his soldiers’ exhaustion and poor condition threatened the plan.

l: duel between Coragus and Dioxippus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Dioxippus fought the Macedonian Coragus in a public single combat. He avoided Coragus’s javelin, broke his sarissa, prevented him from drawing his sword, and knocked him to the ground.

l: Dioxippus's suicide, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: After courtiers arranged for a golden cup to be found under Dioxippus’s cushion and accused him of theft, Dioxippus wrote to Alexander protesting the plot. He then killed himself, and Alexander was greatly troubled by his death.

l: river voyage and shipwrecks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Alexander and his companions sailed down the rivers toward their confluence, where violent whirlpools destroyed or damaged several vessels. Two long ships sank, others were driven ashore, and Alexander’s own ship was caught before he was brought safely to land.

l: siege of the Oxydracee and Mallii capital, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: Alexander ordered an immediate assault on the capital despite Demophoon’s warning. The Macedonian ladders broke when too many men climbed them, leaving Alexander isolated on the wall until Peucestes and other guards reached him.

l: Alexander's wounding, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, After the king had moved from thence, he was informed that
s: During the assault on the capital, Alexander received many blows on his helmet and shield and was finally wounded beneath one breast. He killed the Indian who had wounded him, remained standing with the aid of a tree, and was eventually rescued.
